title: How a phone voice agent holds up in production
subtitle: Calls arrive over SIP and pass through transcription, cleanup, a small open model, typed fields and speech cleanup.
hook: A billion calls a month taught Plivo to collect names and numbers as typed fields, not trust transcripts.

sources.title: 5 Voice Agent Failure Modes You'll Hit in Week One
sources.speaker: Venky B

nodes.label: Caller
nodes.detail: A real person on a phone line. Plivo carries over a billion voice calls a month, which is where these failure patterns show up.
nodes.tradeoff: Most teams aim for under 550 ms to first audio but land between 750 ms and 1.2 s; past that, callers hang up.

nodes.label: SIP trunk
nodes.detail: Plivo runs its own SIP trunking and audio streaming, built over 14 years, so it doesn't rely on anyone else for the telephony or carrier layer.
nodes.tradeoff: The agent on top is a speech pipeline, not a true speech-to-speech product yet.

nodes.label: Speech to text
nodes.detail: Transcribes the call with dynamic keyword boosting: only the names or terms expected at this stage of the call are boosted, then removed.
nodes.tradeoff: Top engines score 4 to 6% word error on known test sets, but noisy, accented real calls end up in double digits.

nodes.label: Transcript cleanup
nodes.detail: An LLM with domain context post-processes the transcript, for example reading an 'E' inside a phone number as a 3, and transliterates code-switched speech.
nodes.tradeoff: Sending consistently cleaned text keeps the agent independent of whichever transcription engine is upstream.

nodes.label: Small open LLM
nodes.detail: Runs with thinking off. Qwen 3.5 or Gemma 4 mixture-of-experts models at 3 to 4B work out of the box; fine-tuning for a domain needs 8 to 12B.
nodes.tradeoff: Frontier APIs sit around 450 to 500 ms p50 to first token and can spike past 1.2 s at p90 to p95.

nodes.label: Self-hosted GPUs
nodes.detail: Plivo hosts open-source models on its own GPUs, which it found the best balance of latency, cost and intelligence when targeting under 300 ms.
nodes.tradeoff: Fast-token clouds like Cerebras or Groq need dedicated capacity booked about 12 months ahead, which is expensive.

nodes.label: Typed fields
nodes.detail: Phone numbers, names and dates are typed fields with validation and allowed values, filled through tool calls and tested like unit tests.
nodes.tradeoff: Thinking in fields instead of free transcripts raised data-collection accuracy from 30% to about 95%.

nodes.label: Speech normalizer
nodes.detail: Sits between the LLM and TTS: strips emojis and markdown, spells out emails, currency and dates, and applies custom pronunciation dictionaries.
nodes.tradeoff: Owning this layer means you can switch TTS providers, say when one is down, without relying on their quirks.

nodes.label: Text to speech
nodes.detail: Speaks the reply back down the line, slowing to about 0.7 to 0.8x speed for entities like emails, phone numbers or spelled-out names.
nodes.tradeoff: The speaker's quick test: if it can't say his surname or 'Plivo' correctly, it will mangle other words too.

flow.text: Reads out a phone number while booking an appointment.
Plivo's SIP trunk streams the call audio into the agent pipeline.
Transcribes with number terms boosted; one digit comes back as 'E'.
An LLM with domain context corrects the 'E' to a 3.
A small open model, thinking off, decides to fill the phone field.
Validates the number against the typed phone field before confirming.
Spells the number out so the voice reads each digit.
Reads the number back slowly so the caller can confirm it.

takeaways.text: Voice agents must run with thinking off, so a year of LLM reasoning gains barely helps them.
Treat collected data as typed, validated fields; Plivo saw accuracy rise from 30% to about 95%.
Boost keywords only at the call stage that needs them; boosting everything makes the transcriber hallucinate.
